title: The Late Period
subtitle: 664–332 BC · The Saite Renaissance, the Persian Conquests and the Last Pharaohs

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: From Psamtik I's reunification and the Saite renaissance through two Persian conquests and the last native pharaohs to Alexander

entries.label: Psamtik I — reunification from Sais
entries.hint: Installed as a local vassal by Assyria after the sack of Thebes, Psamtik I built up his own power in the western Delta, hired Ionian and Carian mercenaries — Herodotus's 'bronze men from the sea' — bought off or absorbed the other Delta princes, and by about 656 controlled all Egypt. He secured Thebes without a fight by having his daughter Nitocris adopted as the next God's Wife of Amun. His 54-year reign restored a single Egyptian state after four centuries of division.
entries.note: Nitocris Adoption Stela (Cairo JE 36327), 656 BC. Herodotus 2.151–54. Alan B. Lloyd, 'The Late Period', in Shaw (ed.), Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000) pp.369–79; Anthony Spalinger, 'Psammetichus, King of Egypt I', JARCE 13 (1976).

entries.label: Necho II — Carchemish and the canal
entries.hint: Necho II marched north to shore up the collapsing Assyrian empire against Babylon — killing King Josiah of Judah at Megiddo on the way — and held Syria briefly before Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed his army at Carchemish in 605 and drove Egypt out of the Levant for good. At home he began digging a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, built a fleet of Greek-style triremes, and, Herodotus says, sent a Phoenician crew to sail around Africa.
entries.note: Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 5) for Carchemish; 2 Kings 23:29, Jeremiah 46. Herodotus 2.158–59 (canal, triremes), 4.42 (circumnavigation). Lloyd in Shaw (2000) pp.371–72.

entries.label: Psamtik II — the raid into Kush
entries.hint: Psamtik II's short reign is remembered for a single campaign: in 593 his army, stiffened with Greek, Carian and Phoenician mercenaries, drove deep into the Kushite kingdom, perhaps as far as Napata, and came home with prisoners and loot. Soldiers scratched their names on the leg of a colossus at Abu Simbel — among the oldest Greek inscriptions anywhere. The blow helped push the Kushite centre of gravity south toward Meroe, and Psamtik had Kushite royal names hacked from Egyptian monuments.
entries.note: Abu Simbel mercenary graffiti: Meiggs & Lewis, A Selection of Greek Historical Inscriptions (1969) no.7. Kush campaign: the Tanis, Karnak and Shellal stelae; Robert Morkot, The Black Pharaohs (2000) pp.296–98; László Török, The Kingdom of Kush (1997) pp.362–69.

entries.label: Apries — the king the army overthrew
entries.hint: Apries — the 'Pharaoh Hophra' of the book of Jeremiah — encouraged Judah to rebel against Babylon and could not save Jerusalem when it fell in 587. He campaigned by sea against Tyre and Sidon, but when an Egyptian army he sent to help settlers against the Greek city of Cyrene was cut to pieces in 570, the native troops mutinied, believing he had spent them to weaken them. His general Amasis was proclaimed king; Apries was captured and killed in 567.
entries.note: Jeremiah 44:30, 37:5–11. Cyrene disaster and mutiny: Herodotus 2.161–63, 169. Amasis stela (Elephantine): translation in Lloyd, Herodotus Book II: Commentary 99–182 (1988). Lloyd in Shaw (2000) pp.372–74.

entries.label: Amasis — forty-four years of prosperity
entries.hint: Amasis, a soldier of common birth, reigned longer than any Saite king in wealth and peace. He concentrated the Greek traders of Egypt at the single port of Naukratis and taxed them, married a woman of Cyrene, sent gifts to Greek temples, and knitted an anti-Persian network with Lydia, Babylon, Sparta and the tyrant Polycrates of Samos. Herodotus tells him as a shrewd, unbuttoned figure — hearing cases in the morning and drinking in the afternoon — and rates his reign Egypt's most prosperous.
entries.note: Herodotus 2.172–82, 3.10–16. Naukratis regulation: Herodotus 2.178–79; Astrid Möller, Naukratis: Trade in Archaic Greece (2000). Lloyd in Shaw (2000) pp.374–76.

entries.label: Psamtik III — six months and the fall
entries.hint: Psamtik III had ruled barely half a year when Cambyses II of Persia invaded. The Egyptian army, its Greek mercenaries partly bought away by a defector, was beaten at Pelusium on the eastern frontier and fell back on Memphis, which was besieged and stormed. Psamtik III was taken to the Persian court, and executed after being implicated in a revolt. The Twenty-sixth Dynasty and Egyptian independence ended together.
entries.note: Herodotus 3.10–15. The mercenary defector Phanes of Halicarnassus: Herodotus 3.4. Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002) pp.52–55.

entries.label: Cambyses II — Egypt becomes a Persian province
entries.hint: Cambyses ruled Egypt as an Egyptian king, taking a pharaonic titulary and, if the courtier Udjahorresnet is to be believed, being coached in Egyptian protocol and expelling foreign squatters from a Saite temple. Later Egyptian and Greek tradition made him a mad sacrilege — stabbing the Apis bull, burning mummies, losing an army in the desert on the way to Siwa — but a contemporary Apis burial dated to his reign shows the bull story is at least exaggerated.
entries.note: Statue of Udjahorresnet (Vatican 22690): Alan B. Lloyd, 'The Inscription of Udjahorresnet', JEA 68 (1982). The Apis stela dated to Cambyses' Year 6 (Louvre): contra Herodotus 3.27–29. The lost army toward Siwa: Herodotus 3.26. Briant (2002) pp.55–61.

entries.label: Darius I — the canal, the law code and Hibis
entries.hint: Darius I governed Egypt through a conciliatory policy: he completed the Nile–Red Sea canal Necho had started, marking it with granite stelae in Old Persian, Elamite, Babylonian and Egyptian; he ordered scholars to compile the laws of Egypt down to the reign of Amasis; and he built the temple of Amun at Hibis in the Kharga Oasis, one of the few temples any Persian king raised. Assessed Egyptian tribute was heavy, and a revolt broke out as he died.
entries.note: Suez canal stelae of Darius: Posener, La première domination perse en Égypte (1936). Law codification: the verso of the Demotic Chronicle (P. BN 215). Hibis temple: Norman de Garis Davies, The Temple of Hibis in El Khārgeh Oasis (1953). Briant (2002) pp.472–84.

entries.label: Xerxes I to Artaxerxes I — revolt and reconquest
entries.hint: Xerxes I put down the revolt of 486 hard and, Herodotus says, treated Egypt more harshly than his father had. The great rising of Inaros of the western Delta from about 460, backed by a large Athenian fleet, held most of Lower Egypt for years before the Persian general Megabyzus crushed it and trapped the Athenians in the marshes. When Herodotus toured Egypt around 450 he found it a Persian province again, and gathered the material for Book Two of his Histories.
entries.note: Herodotus 7.7 (Xerxes), 3.12, 3.15 (Inaros). Thucydides 1.104, 1.109–10 (the Athenian expedition). Herodotus's visit: Alan B. Lloyd, Herodotus Book II: Introduction (1975).

entries.label: Darius II and the end of the first occupation
entries.hint: Under Darius II Persian control loosened. The Aramaic papyri of the Jewish military colony on Elephantine island date mostly to these years — legal deeds, letters, and a request to the Persian and Judaean authorities to rebuild their temple to Yahu, destroyed by a mob with local Egyptian priests' backing in 410. Around 404, as Darius II died and Persia fell into a succession war, Amyrtaeus of Sais led a revolt that made Egypt independent again.
entries.note: Elephantine papyri: Bezalel Porten & Ada Yardeni, Textbook of Aramaic Documents from Ancient Egypt (1986–99); Porten, Archives from Elephantine (1968). The temple-rebuilding petition: TAD A4.7–9. Briant (2002) pp.588–91.

entries.label: Amyrtaeus — the one-king dynasty
entries.hint: Amyrtaeus of Sais, grandson of a leader of an earlier revolt, drove the last Persian garrison out of Egypt and ruled as the sole king of the Twenty-eighth Dynasty, recognised as far south as Aswan by 400. After five years he was defeated and executed — an Aramaic papyrus from Elephantine records the event and the accession of 'Nepherites, king' — and power passed to a rival family from Mendes.
entries.note: Aramaic Papyrus Brooklyn 47.218.152 (the 'Amyrtaeus' papyrus): recording his death 'according to law' and Nepherites' accession. Kienitz, Die politische Geschichte Ägyptens vom 7. bis zum 4. Jahrhundert vor der Zeitwende (1953).

entries.label: Nepherites I and Hakor — independence held with Greek help
entries.hint: The Twenty-ninth Dynasty, from Mendes, kept Egypt free through diplomacy and hired soldiers. Nepherites I allied with Sparta against Persia; his successor Hakor (Achoris) switched to Athens and Evagoras of Cyprus, hired the Athenian general Chabrias, built extensively across Egypt, and beat off a Persian attempt around 385–383. The dynasty ended in a coup after his death, with the throne seized by a general from Sebennytos.
entries.note: Diodorus 14.79, 15.2–4, 15.8–9. Hakor's building: monuments at Karnak, Medinet Habu, Tell el-Maskhuta. Kienitz (1953); Lloyd in Shaw (2000) pp.377–79.

entries.label: Nectanebo I — the invasion of 373 turned back
entries.hint: Nectanebo I of Sebennytos founded the Thirtieth Dynasty and, in 373, faced the largest Persian effort yet — a fleet and army under Pharnabazus with the Athenian Iphicrates commanding the Greek troops. The Persians forced the Mendesian mouth of the Nile but hesitated, quarrelled, and were caught by the rising flood; they withdrew without taking Memphis. Nectanebo I then poured resources into temple-building on a scale not seen since the New Kingdom.
entries.note: Diodorus 15.41–43. The invasion and its failure: John Ray, 'Egypt 525–404 B.C.' and 'Egypt: Dependence and Independence', in Cambridge Ancient History IV and VI (1988–94). Naukratis (Thonis-Heracleion) Decree of Nectanebo I: Franck Goddio's underwater find, 2000.

entries.label: Teos — the offensive that broke on its own cost
entries.hint: Teos took the war to Persia, leading an army into Phoenicia with Greek mercenaries under the aged Spartan king Agesilaus and the Athenian Chabrias. To pay them he taxed the temples and the people heavily and seized temple treasure, which turned opinion against him at home. His own family engineered a coup during the campaign, proclaiming his nephew Nectanebo; Teos fled to the Persian court he had come to fight.
entries.note: Plutarch, Agesilaus 36–40; Xenophon, Agesilaus 2.28–31; Diodorus 15.92–93. Teos's fiscal measures: [Aristotle], Oeconomica 2.2.25a. Lloyd in Shaw (2000) pp.379–80.

entries.label: Nectanebo II — the last pharaoh
entries.hint: Nectanebo II ruled eighteen years, the last Egyptian to hold the throne. He built or added to temples the length of the country, poured patronage into the animal cults, and in 351 turned back a Persian invasion. When Artaxerxes III came again in 343 with a larger force and Greek generals, Nectanebo's defence of the Delta collapsed; he withdrew upriver with the treasury and disappeared, probably into Nubia. Later legend, in the Alexander Romance, made him a magician who fathered Alexander the Great.
entries.note: Diodorus 16.40–51. Building record: the largest of any Late Period king; the Nectanebo II sphinx avenue at Saqqara, the Karnak first pylon. Alexander Romance I.1–14. Ian Moyer, Egypt and the Limits of Hellenism (2011) on the later legend.

entries.label: Artaxerxes III to Mazaces — reconquest and surrender
entries.hint: Artaxerxes III's reconquest in 343 was remembered as a brutal one — walls thrown down, temples plundered, sacred records carried off, and a revived tale of a Persian king killing the Apis. Egypt was a satrapy again for eleven years under a run of governors. The last of them, Mazaces, having no army after the Persian defeat at Issus, handed Egypt to Alexander the Great in 332 without a fight; Alexander sacrificed to the Apis, was crowned at Memphis, and founded Alexandria.
entries.note: Diodorus 16.46–51 (reconquest), 17.49 (Alexander's arrival); Arrian, Anabasis 3.1–5; [Aristotle] Oeconomica 2.2.33–35. Briant (2002) pp.681–90, 1017–19. Alexander at Siwa: Arrian 3.3–4.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The battles of Carchemish and Pelusium, the Nubian campaign, and the wars to keep Persia out of the Nile

entries.label: The end of the Kushite claim
entries.hint: Assyria's withdrawal left Egypt to be reassembled. Psamtik I did it by a mix of force, subsidy and marriage-diplomacy: he neutralised the Delta princes, garrisoned the frontiers with Ionian and Carian troops settled in camps at the Pelusiac mouth, and in 656 secured Thebes bloodlessly through his daughter Nitocris's adoption as heir to the God's Wife of Amun. When Tantamani of Kush died in 653 the Twenty-fifth Dynasty's claim on Egypt died with him.
entries.note: Nitocris Adoption Stela (Cairo JE 36327). The mercenary camps ('the Stratopeda'): Herodotus 2.154. Anthony Spalinger, 'The Concept of the Monarchy during the Saite Epoch', Orientalia 47 (1978).

entries.label: Megiddo and the death of Josiah
entries.hint: When the last Assyrian forces made their stand against Babylon at Harran, Necho II marched an Egyptian army north to help them. King Josiah of Judah moved to block the pass at Megiddo and was killed there, an event the books of Kings and Chronicles treat as a national catastrophe. Necho pressed on, imposed a tribute on Judah and installed a client king, and held the Levant as far as the Euphrates for four years.
entries.note: 2 Kings 23:29–35; 2 Chronicles 35:20–24; Jeremiah 22:10–12. Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3–4. Nadav Na'aman, 'The Kingdom of Judah under Josiah', Tel Aviv 18 (1991).

entries.label: The Battle of Carchemish
entries.hint: At Carchemish the Babylonian crown prince Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Necho II's field army and pursued the survivors south; a follow-up victory at Hamath finished the campaign. Egypt lost Syria and Palestine permanently and never again projected land power beyond Sinai except as a raider. The Babylonian Chronicle's terse account — the Egyptian army 'withdrew before him' and 'was beaten and could not escape' — marks the end of Egypt as a great power in the Near East.
entries.note: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 5 (BM 21946); Jeremiah 46:2–12. D.J. Wiseman, Chronicles of Chaldaean Kings (1956); Israel Ephʿal, The City Besieged (2009).

entries.label: Psamtik II's expedition into Kush
entries.hint: In his third year Psamtik II sent an army under the general Potasimto and the Egyptian commander Amasis, its ranks full of Greek, Carian and Phoenician mercenaries, up the Nile against Kush. It defeated a Kushite force and raided deep — a stela claims the taking of a place read as Pnubs or beyond, near Napata. Homesick soldiers cut their names into a colossus at Abu Simbel. The raid did no lasting damage but confirmed the Kushite retreat toward Meroe.
entries.note: Karnak, Tanis and Shellal stelae of Psamtik II: Sauneron & Yoyotte, 'La campagne nubienne de Psammétique II', BIFAO 50 (1952). Abu Simbel graffiti: Meiggs & Lewis, GHI no.7.

entries.label: The Battle of Pelusium
entries.hint: Cambyses II crossed Sinai with Arab help arranging water in the desert, and met the Egyptian army under Psamtik III at Pelusium, the fortress guarding the eastern approach. The Egyptians were beaten and fell back on Memphis, which surrendered after a siege. Herodotus, who saw the battlefield, reports the bones of the two armies still lying separate decades later, and tells a story of Cambyses driving cats and other sacred animals before his troops so the Egyptians would not shoot.
entries.note: Herodotus 3.10–13. Polyaenus 7.9 (the animal-shields story). Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002) pp.52–55.

entries.label: The revolt of Inaros
entries.loc: Memphis (the White Castle) / the Delta marshes
entries.hint: Inaros, a Libyan dynast of the western Delta, raised most of Lower Egypt against Persia and called in Athens, then at war with Persia, which sent about two hundred ships. The rebels beat a Persian army, killed the satrap Achaemenes, and penned the survivors in the fortified quarter of Memphis for eighteen months. The Persian general Megabyzus broke the siege, drove the Athenians onto an island in the Nile and forced their surrender; a relief squadron was ambushed. Inaros was crucified.
entries.note: Thucydides 1.104, 1.109–10; Herodotus 3.12, 3.15; Ctesias, Persica F14. Analysis: Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002) pp.573–77; Kahn, 'Inaros' Rebellion against Artaxerxes I', Classical Quarterly 58 (2008).

entries.label: The invasion of 373 BC repelled
entries.loc: the Mendesian mouth of the Nile
entries.hint: After decades of failed attempts, Persia sent its largest force yet against independent Egypt: perhaps 200,000 men and 300 triremes under the satrap Pharnabazus, with the Athenian Iphicrates leading the Greek mercenaries. They landed at the Mendesian mouth and took a fort, but Pharnabazus refused Iphicrates' plan to rush Memphis, the two fell out, the Nile flood rose, and the army re-embarked and left. It was the high-water mark of the last native Egyptian state.
entries.note: Diodorus 15.41–43; Cornelius Nepos, Iphicrates 2. John Ray in Cambridge Ancient History VI (1994) ch.4; Lloyd in Shaw (2000) pp.378–79.

entries.label: The reconquest of 343 and Alexander's arrival
entries.hint: Artaxerxes III's third invasion, in 343, broke through: Greek mercenary generals on the Persian side outmanoeuvred Nectanebo II's forward defence, the frontier towns fell, and the last pharaoh withdrew south and vanished. Persia held Egypt for eleven bitter years, its temples looted and its walls slighted. When Alexander the Great reached the frontier in 332, the Persian satrap Mazaces, left without an army after Issus, simply handed the country over; Alexander was welcomed as a liberator.
entries.note: Diodorus 16.40–51; [Aristotle] Oeconomica 2.2.33–35; Arrian, Anabasis 3.1. The looting of temples and records: the Satrap Stela (Cairo CG 22182) and Ptolemaic tradition. Briant (2002) pp.685–90.
